paragraphs.text: Polymicrogyria with or without vascular-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic COL3A1 mutations. The brain phenotype consists of bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria of the cobblestone variant, cerebellar microcysts, and white matter abnormalities, and resembles that of individuals with recessive GPR56 mutations. Some affected individuals also have a severe Ehlers-Danlos syndrome phenotype with vascular fragility. The phenotype varies among patients (Horn et al., 2017; Vandervore et al., 2017).

paragraphs.text: Jørgensen et al. (2015) reported 2 sibs with vascular EDS. The proband (III-2), a boy, was born with a right-sided clubfoot and developed a unilateral hydrocele of the testis. He had crowded teeth, retrognathia, long slender fingers, and pale, translucent skin with visible subcutaneous vessels. His facial features were characteristic of EDS type IV, with a small lower jaw, prominent eyes, a pinched nose, and a thin upper lip. He died at 15 years of age. Autopsy showed 3 dissections: a transverse dissection of nearly the whole circumference of the thoracic aorta at the level of the ligamentum arteriosus, and separate dissections of the right renal artery and the left femoral artery. There was cystic medial necrosis of the aortic wall, and no macroscopic brain anomalies were found. His sister (III-3) was evaluated at 19 years of age. She had cerebral cortical dysplasia with bilaterally thickened frontoparietal cortices and small gyri, findings consistent with pachy micropolygyria. Her cognitive functioning was normal, a recent neurologic examination was normal, and she had never had epileptic seizures. MR arteriography and CT angiography showed a stenotic process in the right internal carotid artery, which ultrasonography showed to be a dissection. The left internal carotid artery was ectatic, and the right external iliac artery was stenotic. She had the same skin and facial features as her brother, with spontaneous ruptures of superficial vessels, long slender fingers, hypermobility of the small joints of the hands, and crowded teeth. Other findings included rupture of the medial meniscus and anterior cruciate ligament, intermittent abdominal pain, diarrhea, and blood in the stool with increased wall thickness of the transverse colon, migraine with aura, and minimal mitral leakage. She did not have aortic dilatation or varicose veins. Heterozygous carriers in the family varied markedly. The father, who carried a nonsense variant, had no abnormal findings at age 63, and paternal relatives with the same variant had no features of vascular EDS. The mother, who carried a missense variant, had thin skin, visible vessels, and reduced elasticity of the ascending aorta, but by age 60 she did not have the complete picture of vascular EDS.

paragraphs.text: Vandervore et al. (2017) studied a family with 2 affected and 2 unaffected sibs. Brain MRI in the affected sibs showed a cobblestone-like cortical malformation, white matter changes, and cerebellar cysts. The authors also reviewed brain imaging of 2 previously reported individuals with biallelic COL3A1 mutations. The brain phenotype in all of these patients was similar to that associated with GPR56 mutations, and all 3 families reported to date had a cobblestone-like malformation.

In a second family, 2 affected sibs had a cobblestone-like cortical malformation, cerebellar cysts, white matter abnormalities, developmental delay, and seizures. Horn et al. (2017) also considered 3 previously reported families. All families with biallelic COL3A1 variants had specific structural brain anomalies, and some had a severe EDS phenotype. The brain phenotype consisted of bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria of the cobblestone variant, cerebellar microcysts, and white matter abnormalities, and resembled that of individuals with recessive GPR56 mutations.

paragraphs.text: Schwarze et al. (2001) studied 4 probands whose presenting feature was vascular aneurysm or rupture. They identified 3 heterozygous frameshift mutations in the COL3A1 gene (1832delAA, 413delC, and 555delT), which led to premature termination codons in exons 27, 6, and 9, respectively. A fourth patient carried a heterozygous nonsense mutation in the final exon (4294C-T; R1432X). The mRNAs from the frameshift alleles were transcribed efficiently but degraded rapidly, presumably by nonsense-mediated decay. The mRNA from the final-exon mutation was stable, but the truncated protein it encoded was not incorporated into mature type III procollagen molecules. The authors concluded that, unlike null mutations in COL1A1 and COL2A1, null mutations in COL3A1 produce phenotypes that overlap with vascular EDS.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with vascular EDS, Jørgensen et al. (2015) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the COL3A1 gene. One was a c.1786C-T transition resulting in an arg596-to-ter (R596X) substitution, inherited from the father; the other was G1284E, inherited from the mother. The brother died at 15 years with aortic, renal, and femoral artery dissections. The sister had bilateral frontoparietal pachy micropolygyria and an internal carotid artery dissection. The father, who was heterozygous for R596X, had no abnormal findings at age 63, and his fibroblasts produced a reduced amount of apparently normal type III procollagen.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with vascular EDS, one of whom had bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria, Jørgensen et al. (2015) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the COL3A1 gene: a c.3851G-A transition resulting in a gly1284-to-glu (G1284E) substitution, inherited from the mother, and R596X, inherited from the father. G1284E was predicted to alter a highly conserved residue in the C-propeptide, within a calcium-binding region next to a cysteine involved in interchain disulfide bonding, and to slow trimer assembly. Fibroblasts from the compound heterozygous patient produced a reduced amount of overmodified type III procollagen. The heterozygous mother had thin skin, visible vessels, and reduced elasticity of the ascending aorta.
